title: Is 1 kg of flour still 1 kg on the Moon?
hook: Gravity on the Moon is a sixth of Earth's. Does your bag of flour lose anything?

knows: a bag of flour is sold as 1 kg
the Moon has weaker gravity than Earth
what a kitchen balance and a spring scale look like
doesNotKnow: the difference between mass and weight
the newton as a unit of force

misconception: Mass and weight are the same thing, so the flour's mass (its kilograms) drops on the Moon.
objective: The learner can explain that mass (how much stuff) stays the same everywhere, while weight (how hard a world pulls on it) is mass times the local gravity, and that a spring scale measures weight while a balance compares masses.

claims.text: Weight is mass times the local gravity, W = m g; a 1 kg bag weighs 9.81 N on Earth and 1.62 N on the Moon.
claims.source: Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5 (weight). 1 x 9.81 = 9.81 N; 1 x 1.62 = 1.62 N.

claims.text: Surface gravity: Earth 9.81, Moon 1.62, Mars 3.73 and Jupiter 23.12 m/s^2 (Jupiter has no solid surface; its value is at the 1 bar pressure level, at the equator).
claims.source: NASA Goddard fact sheets (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/): Moon gravity 1.62; Mars fact sheet mean surface gravity 3.73 (equatorial 3.69); Jupiter fact sheet equatorial gravity at 1 bar 23.12 (mean 25.92 without rotation, polar 27.01). Earth: standard gravity 9.80665, shown as 9.81 (BIPM). v2 changed from 3.71 / 24.79 after the 2026-10-13 fact-check found the cited source did not contain those figures. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): NASA NSSDC fact sheets via search (direct fetch blocked): Jupiter equatorial gravity at 1 bar 23.12 (mean 25.92, polar 27.01); Mars mean 3.73 (equatorial 3.69); Moon 1.62; Earth standard 9.80665 shown 9.81. Note ESA/Wikipedia give 24.79 for Jupiter at 1 bar, a different reference; 23.12 is the NASA equatorial figure and is labelled as such.

claims.text: A spring scale measures the pull of gravity (a force), so its reading changes from world to world; a balance compares two masses in the same gravity, so it stays level anywhere.
claims.source: Spring: Hooke's law F = k x, stretch proportional to weight m g. Balance: torques m1 g d = m2 g d, g cancels, so equal masses balance for any g.

claims.text: Mass, how much stuff there is, stays 1 kg anywhere.
claims.source: Mass is an intrinsic property of the object, independent of location (SI definition of the kilogram, BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed.).

claims.text: A bathroom scale is a spring scale marked in kg for Earth: on the Moon it shows about a sixth of its Earth reading.
claims.source: Bathroom scales measure force through a spring or strain gauge and display it as kg assuming Earth gravity; 1.62 / 9.81 = 0.165, about one sixth. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Bathroom scales measure force (spring or strain-gauge load cell) and are calibrated in kg for Earth; 1.62/9.81 = 0.165, about a sixth. 'Is a spring scale' is loose for strain-gauge scales but the behaviour claimed holds for both.

claims.text: Gravity at the Moon's surface is about a sixth of Earth's.
claims.source: 1.62 / 9.81 = 0.165, about 1/6 (values from c2, NASA Planetary Fact Sheet).

claims.text: A spring scale marked in kg for Earth's gravity shows a 1 kg bag as 0.17 kg on the Moon, 0.38 kg on Mars and 2.36 kg on Jupiter; the pull there is 17%, 38% and 236% of Earth's.
claims.source: Shown kg = m g / 9.81 (a spring reading divided by Earth's g): 1.62/9.81 = 0.165, 3.73/9.81 = 0.380, 23.12/9.81 = 2.357. Gravity values from c2. Computed in Demo.tsx from the same WORLDS table that draws the spring. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: g/9.81 = 0.165, 0.380, 2.357 -> 0.17, 0.38, 2.36 kg and 17%, 38%, 236%; matches Demo.tsx toFixed(2) and pct. NASA ratio to Earth for Jupiter 2.364 (eq.) is consistent.

recall.question: An astronaut's mass is 70 kg on Earth. On Mars, where gravity is weaker, what is her mass?
recall.why: Mass is how much stuff there is and does not change with location; only weight, the pull of gravity, is smaller on Mars.
